clinicalPearls: A benign fibroepithelial polyp that typically arises from the posterior (prostatic) urethra near the verumontanum
In boys it classically causes intermittent obstructive voiding, haematuria, or a polyp that prolapses into the bladder neck and produces intermittent obstruction
In adults it may cause haematuria, haematospermia, voiding symptoms, or be found incidentally
It is a recognised benign cause of lower urinary tract symptoms and, when near the prostate, may be associated with PSA elevation as a benign mimic of malignancy
Cystourethroscopy demonstrates a mobile pedunculated lesion, and urethrography may show a corresponding filling defect
Histology shows a fibrovascular core covered by urothelium without malignant features
Treatment is endoscopic transurethral resection, which is usually curative
reference.pathophysiology: A posterior urethral polyp is a benign proliferation with a fibrovascular core lined by normal urothelium, generally considered congenital in boys and arising on a stalk near the verumontanum. Its mobility on a pedicle allows intermittent prolapse into the bladder neck, producing positional or intermittent obstruction, while surface trauma explains episodes of haematuria and haematospermia.
additionalDifferentials: Prostatic-type urethral polyp with prostatic epithelium
Prostatic adenocarcinoma as a PSA-raising mimic
additionalInvestigations: Cystourethroscopy to visualise and localise the polyp
Voiding or retrograde urethrography showing a mobile filling defect
Urinalysis and urine cytology to assess haematuria
Pelvic MRI or ultrasound if a mass or malignancy is suspected
Histopathology of the resected specimen for definitive diagnosis
PSA interpreted cautiously, recognising the possibility of benign elevation
redFlags: Persistent haematuria or atypical cytology suggesting urothelial malignancy
A rising or persistently elevated PSA warranting exclusion of prostate cancer
reference.prognosis: Excellent; endoscopic resection is generally curative with a low recurrence rate, and the typical fibroepithelial polyp is benign with no malignant potential.
pitfalls: Attributing a raised PSA to the polyp and missing a coexisting prostate cancer
Mistaking the polyp for posterior urethral valves in a child
Incomplete resection of the stalk leading to recurrence
Failing to send tissue for histology to exclude malignancy
management: Perform endoscopic transurethral resection or excision of the polyp, which is generally curative
Relieve any acute obstruction from a polyp prolapsing into the bladder neck with catheter drainage before definitive resection
Send the resected specimen for histopathology to confirm a benign fibroepithelial polyp and exclude malignancy
Undertake surveillance cystourethroscopy for the low risk of recurrence
Interpret PSA cautiously, recognising benign elevation as a mimic of prostate malignancy
Refer to urology, or paediatric urology in boys, for endoscopic management
